rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).
criteria_text: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as the position, which matches the required verdict in criterion 1.

The answer explicitly states that the technical documentation must include 'a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run', citing Annex IV point 1(e), which conveys the substance of the requirement.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No, the AI system is not "medium-risk"; it is high-risk, and Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 operates no "medium-risk" tier into which it could fall. Classification follows Article 6(1), whose two conditions are cumulative and both met here: under point (a) the AI system is intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and the Medical Devices Regulation is Annex I, point 11; under point (b) that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market, which the operator's device does. Article 6(1) applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the device. The device's sectoral risk class is not transposed onto the AI system: Article 6(1)(b) asks only whether a third-party assessment is required, not which class triggered it. Consequently the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements apply (Articles 8 and 9), and under Article 43(3) they are assessed within the MDR notified-body procedure, with Annex VII points 4.3 to 4.6 also applying, and Article 8(2) permitting integration into existing MDR documentation.
criteria_text: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification
criterion_remarks: Answer correctly states that the AI system is high-risk and that the EU AI Act has no 'medium-risk' category
Answer states the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, specifically the Medical Devices Regulation
Answer confirms the product undergoes third-party conformity assessment as required under Article 6(1)(b)
Answer explains that both conditions are cumulative under Article 6(1) and applies irrespective of the device's sectoral classification
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information in a coherent, actionable manner

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: No, the system is not prohibited, and it is not high‑risk on the Annex III route. Article 5(1) lists no prohibition covering one‑to‑one biometric verification; points (d) and (g) concern criminal‑offence risk assessment and biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes, neither of which this system performs. Annex III, point 1(a) expressly excludes from remote biometric identification "AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification the sole purpose of which is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be", so Article 6(2) is not engaged and no Article 6(3) derogation assessment is needed. High‑risk status could still arise under Article 6(1) if the system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I. The evidence supplied contains no text for Article 12(2), points (a) to (c), so no logging duties can be stated here.
criteria_text: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the system is not prohibited and correctly explains that Article 5(1) does not cover one-to-one biometric verification, distinguishing prohibited uses.
The answer states the system is not high-risk under Annex III, correctly explaining that the exclusion in Annex III.1(a) applies, so Article 6(2) is not engaged.
The answer directly quotes and applies the exclusion in Annex III.1(a) for biometric verification with the sole purpose of confirming identity, confirming the system falls within it.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents reasoning in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Human oversight is governed by Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Article 14(1) requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons while in use; Article 14(2) directs that oversight aim to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety or fundamental rights arising from intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse. Under Article 14(3) the measures must be commensurate with the risks, autonomy and context of use, and be built into the system by the provider or identified for the deployer to implement. Article 14(4) requires enabling overseers to understand capacities and limitations, counter automation bias, interpret output correctly, disregard, override or reverse it, and intervene or halt the system safely. Article 14(5) adds separate confirmation by two competent natural persons for Annex III point 1(a) remote biometric identification, unless disproportionate under Union or national law for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum.
criteria_text: Article 14
Design for effective human oversight during use
Aim: prevent/minimise risks to health, safety, fundamental rights
Measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer
Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that human oversight is governed by Article 14.
The answer states that high-risk AI systems must be designed to be effectively overseen during use, capturing the substance of Article 14(1).
The answer specifies that oversight aims to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights from intended use or foreseeable misuse, reflecting Article 14(2).
The answer describes oversight measures as either built into the system by the provider or identified for implementation by the deployer, matching Article 14(3).

The answer lists all key capabilities overseers must have: understanding, monitoring, countering automation bias, interpreting output, overriding, and halting the system, covering all elements of Article 14(4).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.
criteria_text: Yes, exceptions exist
Condition: model released under free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution
Condition: parameters (weights, architecture info, usage info) made publicly available
Exception covers only points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), not (c)/(d)
Exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
criterion_remarks: The answer affirms the existence of exceptions in Article 53(2).
The answer states the model must be released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification, and distribution.
The answer specifies that parameters, including weights, architecture, and usage information, must be made publicly available.
The answer clearly limits the exception to points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), and explicitly states that (c) and (d) still apply.
The answer states the exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, which remain subject to full obligations.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in a coherent, regulatory-appropriate manner without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the AI practices prohibited by Article 5 is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). This is the highest of the three ceilings in the penalty regime, reflecting the gravity of the Article 5 prohibitions, and it applies to the placing on the market, putting into service or use of any of the practices listed in Article 5(1). Where the offender is an SME, including a start-up, the applicable ceiling is the lower of the percentage and the fixed amount rather than the higher (Article 99(6)). Member States must ensure the penalties are effective, proportionate and dissuasive, and each fine must take into account the gravity and nature of the infringement and the circumstances listed in Article 99(7). The lower ceilings, EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % under Article 99(4), and EUR 7 500 000 or 1 % under Article 99(5), expressly do not apply to Article 5 breaches. The engaged evidence contains no material on Annex III, Article 27 or Article 43 relevant to this question.
criteria_text: EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
Applies to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the fine amount as EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The candidate answer explicitly states that the fines apply to non-compliance with the AI practices prohibited by Article 5, satisfying the substance of criterion 2.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; well-structured and coherent prose suitable for a regulatory compliance context.

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: ‘deep fake’ means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful;
criteria_text: AI-generated or manipulated content
Image, audio, or video
Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events
Falsely appears authentic or truthful to a person
criterion_remarks: The answer states that deep fakes are AI-generated or manipulated content, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies image, audio or video content, which matches the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the content resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events, which matches the substance of criterion 3.
The answer states the content would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful, which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: The response is in neutral, professional language, directly quoting the definition from the Act in a clear and concise manner suitable for a regulatory context.

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.
criteria_text: Unacceptable risk - prohibited practices (Article 5)
High risk - Article 6, referencing Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases)
Limited risk - transparency obligations (Article 50)
Minimal or no risk - no mandatory obligations, voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5, conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer identifies high-risk systems under Article 6 and references both Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases), capturing the full substance of the criterion.
The answer states that limited-risk systems carry transparency duties under Article 50, which matches the substance of the criterion.
The answer notes that minimal-risk systems avoid high-risk obligations and mentions voluntary codes of conduct under Article 95, thereby stating the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose suitable for regulatory advice; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).
criteria_text: Yes
Putting own name/trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service (Article 25(1)(a))
Substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service that remains high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(b))
Modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk (incl. general-purpose) AI system such that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(c))
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word, clearly affirming the possibility.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(a) by explaining that putting one's name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market results in being considered a provider.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(b) by describing substantial modification of a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk as a triggering condition.

The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(c) by explaining that modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk results in provider status.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: Under Article 1(1), the Regulation's objective is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation. Article 1(2) then specifies the harmonised rules serving that objective.
criteria_text: Improve functioning of the internal market
Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the objective includes improving the functioning of the internal market.
The answer explicitly states the objective of promoting the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI.
The answer includes the full scope of protection—health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and environmental protection—against harmful effects of AI systems.
The answer explicitly mentions supporting innovation as part of the objective.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose that clearly conveys the regulatory content without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).
criteria_text: No
Falls under narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a)
Exception: remains high-risk if system performs profiling of natural persons
Provider must document the assessment before placing on market/putting into service (Article 6(4))
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No' as the initial verdict, which matches the required 'No' in criterion 1 and is unambiguous.

The answer explicitly states that structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task and cites the correct provision, Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a), satisfying the substance of the criterion.

The answer clearly excludes profiling of natural persons from the derogation by stating 'the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons', which captures the exception in the criterion.
The answer references Article 6(4) and states the provider must document the assessment before market placement or putting into service, which matches the requirement in the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; well-structured and coherent prose suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: Under Article 101(5) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review decisions of the Commission fixing a fine under Article 101, and it may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed. That unlimited jurisdiction means the Court is not confined to reviewing legality but may substitute its own assessment of the amount for the Commission's, including raising it above the level the Commission set, subject to the ceiling in Article 101(1) of 3 % of annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher. In exercising it the Court applies the same standards binding on the Commission: the fine must reflect the nature, gravity and duration of the infringement with due account of proportionality and appropriateness (Article 101(1)) and must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive (Article 101(3)).
criteria_text: Unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine
Court may cancel the fine
Court may reduce the fine
Court may increase the fine
criterion_remarks: The answer states the Court has 'unlimited jurisdiction to review decisions of the Commission fixing a fine', which conveys the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly states the Court 'may cancel, reduce or increase the fine', satisfying the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes 'may ... reduce the fine', directly stating the substance of criterion 3.
The answer states the Court 'may ... increase the fine', including that it may substitute a higher amount, which satisfies the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with logically structured and grammatically complete prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: Under Article 49(1) a provider (or, where applicable, its authorised representative) must, before placing the system on the market or putting it into service, register itself and the system in the EU database, entering the Section A data of Annex VIII (Article 71(2)). Those items are: the provider's name, address and contact details; where submission is made by another person on the provider's behalf, that person's name, address and contact details; the authorised representative's name, address and contact details, where applicable; the AI system's trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing its identification and traceability; a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported through the system; a basic and concise description of the information used by the system (data, inputs) and its operating logic; the status of the system (on the market or in service; no longer placed on the market or in service; recalled); the type, number and expiry date of the notified body's certificate and that body's name or identification number, where applicable; a scanned copy of that certificate, where applicable; the Member States in which the system is or has been placed on the market, put into service or made available in the Union; a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; electronic instructions for use, which are not provided for high-risk systems in the law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control areas of Annex III, points 1, 6 and 7; and, optionally, a URL for additional information. For those same law enforcement, migration, asylum and border-control systems, registration is made in a secure non-public section of the database (Article 49(4)).
criteria_text: Contact details of the provider, of any person submitting on its behalf and of the authorised representative, where applicable (Annex VIII, Section A, points 1 to 3)
AI system trade name and an unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability (point 4)
Intended purpose and the components and functions the system supports (point 5)
Basic and concise description of the data and inputs used and the operating logic (point 6)
Market status and the notified body certificate details with a scanned copy, where applicable (points 7 to 9)
Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the electronic instructions for use (points 10 to 12)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly lists the contact details of the provider, any person submitting on its behalf, and the authorised representative where applicable.
The answer includes the trade name and an unambiguous reference for identification and traceability.
The answer states the requirement to describe the intended purpose and the components and functions supported by the system.
The answer provides a clear statement about the need for a basic and concise description of the data, inputs, and operating logic.
The answer covers the system's market status and all applicable certificate details including type, number, expiry date, notified body ID, and scanned copy.
The answer includes the Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity, and electronic instructions for use, noting the exception for certain high-risk systems.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.
criteria_text: Language: drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established
Validity period stated: not exceeding five years (Annex I systems) or four years (Annex III systems)
criterion_remarks: The answer states the certificate must be drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies that the validity period may not exceed five years for Annex I systems and four years for Annex III systems, conveying the substance of criterion 2.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).
criteria_text: Only where strictly necessary for bias detection/correction under Art 10(2)(f)-(g), and cannot be effectively achieved with other data (incl. synthetic/anonymised)
Technical re-use limitations plus state-of-the-art security/privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive
criterion_remarks: Answer states processing is allowed only when strictly necessary and cannot be effectively fulfilled with other data, including synthetic or anonymised.
Answer includes technical limitations on re-use and specifies state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation.
Answer covers strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations and prohibits transmission or access by others.
Answer explicitly states deletion upon bias correction or end of retention period, whichever comes first.
Answer notes that records must document the necessity and why other data types would not suffice.
Answer clarifies that the conditions are in addition to, not a substitute for, GDPR, EUDPR, and the Law Enforcement Directive.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in clear, coherent prose suitable for regulatory use.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Under Article 13(3) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, a provider must accompany a high-risk AI system with concise, complete, correct and clear instructions for use containing at least six categories of information. First, the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative (Article 13(3)(a)). Second, the characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, including intended purpose, accuracy (with metrics), robustness and cybersecurity levels, known or foreseeable circumstances giving rise to risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, technical capabilities to explain output, performance for specific persons or groups, input-data specifications, and, where appropriate, information enabling deployers to interpret output (Article 13(3)(b)). Third, changes to the system and its performance pre-determined at initial conformity assessment (Article 13(3)(c)). Fourth, the human oversight measures under Article 14, including technical measures facilitating interpretation of outputs (Article 13(3)(d)). Fifth, computational and hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance and care measures, including frequency and software updates (Article 13(3)(e)). Sixth, where relevant, a description of mechanisms enabling deployers to collect, store and interpret the logs under Article 12 (Article 13(3)(f)).
criteria_text: Provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity/contact details

Characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input data specifications)
Pre-determined changes to the system and its performance
Human oversight measures under Article 14
Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity and contact details as required by Article 13(3)(a).

The answer includes all listed sub-elements of Article 13(3)(b), such as intended purpose, accuracy metrics, robustness, cybersecurity, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, and input data specifications.
The answer clearly mentions pre-determined changes to the system and its performance at the time of initial conformity assessment as required by Article 13(3)(c).
The answer references human oversight measures under Article 14 and includes technical measures to facilitate interpretation of outputs, satisfying Article 13(3)(d).
The answer covers computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime, and maintenance measures including frequency and software updates as required by Article 13(3)(e).
The answer includes, where relevant, a description of mechanisms for log collection, storage, and interpretation under Article 12, as specified in Article 13(3)(f).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with logical flow and no self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by the organisations representing them, or by both, while the AI Office and the Member States are the bodies that must encourage and facilitate their drawing up (Article 95(1) and (3)). Under Article 95(3), drawing up may involve any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society organisations and academia, and a code may cover one or more AI systems having regard to the similarity of their intended purpose. Article 95(1) directs that encouragement and facilitation towards codes, including related governance mechanisms, fostering voluntary application to non-high-risk AI systems of some or all Chapter III, Section 2 requirements. Article 95(2) adds that the same two bodies facilitate codes on voluntary application, including by deployers, of specific requirements to all AI systems on the basis of clear objectives and key performance indicators. Article 95(4) requires them to take account of SMEs' and start-ups' interests and needs.
criteria_text: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or both
May involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia
The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct
criterion_remarks: The answer states that codes may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers, by organisations representing them, or by both, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer explicitly mentions that drawing up may involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia, satisfying criterion 2.
The answer clearly identifies the AI Office and the Member States as the bodies required to encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, directly satisfying criterion 3.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Under Article 17(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, a provider of a high-risk AI system must put in place a quality management system ensuring compliance with the Regulation, documented in a systematic and orderly manner as written policies, procedures and instructions, covering at least thirteen aspects. (a) A strategy for regulatory compliance, including conformity assessment procedures and management of modifications to the system. (b) Techniques, procedures and systematic actions for design, design control and design verification. (c) The same for development, quality control and quality assurance. (d) Examination, test and validation procedures before, during and after development, and their frequency. (k) Record-keeping systems and procedures. (l) Resource management, including security-of-supply measures. (m) An accountability framework setting out management and staff responsibilities for all those aspects. Implementation must be proportionate to the provider's organisation size, without lowering the rigour and protection required (Article 17(2)).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Under Article 5(1)(h) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes is prohibited unless and in so far as strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives. First, Article 5(1)(h)(i): the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons. Second, Article 5(1)(h)(ii): the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack. Third, Article 5(1)(h)(iii): the localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence, for the purpose of conducting a criminal investigation or prosecution or executing a criminal penalty, for offences referred to in Annex II punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order for a maximum period of at least four years.
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, and missing persons, matching the substance of criterion 1.
The answer includes the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, as well as a genuine terrorist threat, capturing the full substance of criterion 2.

The answer specifies the localisation or identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or execution of a penalty for Annex II offences punishable by at least four years’ sentence, which matches criterion 3 in substance.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear legal prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Article 50(2) governs. Providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The technical solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, but only as far as is technically feasible, taking into account the specificities and limitations of the various types of content, the costs of implementation and the generally acknowledged state of the art, as may be reflected in relevant technical standards. The duty does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the deployer's input data or its semantics, or where authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.

Marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated
Solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, as far as technically feasible
Feasibility judged against content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art
Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation
criterion_remarks: The answer states that outputs must be marked in a machine-readable format.
The answer explicitly says outputs must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
The answer includes that the solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible.
The answer references content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and the state of the art as factors for feasibility.
The answer lists all three exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input/semantics, and law-enforcement authorisation.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: The Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V, and it entrusts the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office (Article 88(1)). That exclusivity covers the whole of Chapter V, so the obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models under Article 53, including, for models with systemic risk, the Article 55(1) duties of model evaluation with adversarial testing, assessment and mitigation of Union-level systemic risks, reporting of serious incidents to the AI Office, and adequate cybersecurity protection of the model and its physical infrastructure, are enforced centrally rather than by national market surveillance authorities. The Commission must exercise those powers taking into account the procedural guarantees under Article 94, and the delegation to the AI Office is without prejudice to the Commission's own powers of organisation and to the division of competences between the Member States and the Union under the Treaties (Article 88(1)). Market surveillance authorities retain no enforcement role over Chapter V; they may only request the Commission to exercise those powers where necessary and proportionate to assist with their own tasks (Article 88(2)). Providers must cooperate with the Commission and national competent authorities in the exercise of those competences (Article 53(3)).

AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer explicitly states that the Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Data collected and processed for the purpose of testing high-risk AI systems in real world conditions may be transferred to third countries only provided that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented (Article 60(4)(e)). That condition is not free-standing: it is one of the cumulative conditions in Article 60(4), all of which must be met for the provider or prospective provider to conduct the testing at all, so the transfer safeguard operates only where the real-world testing plan has been submitted and approved, the testing has been registered, the provider is established in the Union or has appointed a Union-established legal representative, and the remaining conditions of that paragraph are satisfied (Article 60(4)). The evidence supplied contains no text for Article 10(5), points (a) to (f), so no condition can be attributed to it here.
criteria_text: Appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the substance of the criterion by explicitly requiring that 'appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented' for data transfers, which directly reflects the requirement in Article 60(4)(e).
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and uses precise regulatory language without self-reference, hedging, or informality; well-structured and logically ordered.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No, the conditions are alternatives, not cumulative. Article 51(1) provides that a general-purpose AI model is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk if it meets any of the following conditions: (a) it has high-impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks; or (b) based on a decision of the Commission, taken ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, it has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those in point (a), having regard to the criteria set out in Annex XIII. Meeting either limb alone triggers classification. Within limb (a), Article 51(2) adds a rebuttable presumption: a model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities where the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating-point operations, is greater than 10^25. Under Article 51(3) the Commission may amend those thresholds and supplement the benchmarks and indicators by delegated act to reflect the state of the art. Classification triggers the Article 55(1) obligations in addition to Article 53.
criteria_text: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of condition (a), including the 10^25 FLOPs rebuttable presumption as specified in Article 51(2).
The answer clearly explains condition (b), including the Commission's role and reference to Annex XIII criteria, based on either ex officio action or a qualified alert.
The answer explicitly states that the conditions are alternatives, not cumulative, and that meeting either limb suffices.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality while clearly conveying regulatory content.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No. Both conditions in Article 6(1) must be fulfilled cumulatively, and only one is met here. Article 6(1)(a) is satisfied: the system is a safety component of a product covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745, listed in Annex I, point 11. But Article 6(1)(b) is not: a Class I device that is non-sterile, without a measuring function and not a reusable surgical instrument is self-certified by the manufacturer and is not required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under the MDR. The system is therefore high-risk only if it separately falls within a listed use-case of Annex III under Article 6(2).
criteria_text: No
Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the conclusion, matching the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that both conditions in Article 6(1) must be fulfilled cumulatively, capturing the substance of the criterion.
The answer correctly explains that the specified MDR Class I device is self-certified and does not require third-party conformity assessment.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a lift can be a high-risk AI system, provided the two cumulative conditions in Article 6(1) are both met, and this is so irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift. First, under Article 6(1)(a), the AI system must be intended to be used as a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; lifts and safety components for lifts are covered by Directive 2014/33/EU, listed at Annex I, point 4. Second, under Article 6(1)(b), the lift whose safety component the AI system is must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that Directive. This is the Annex I product route, so the Article 6(3) derogation, which applies only to Annex III systems, is unavailable. Conformity assessment then follows Article 43(3), under the procedure required by Directive 2014/33/EU.
criteria_text: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its unambiguous position.
The answer states the AI system must be intended as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, and specifies lifts are covered by Directive 2014/33/EU in Annex I.
The answer states the product (the lift) must be required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the applicable Annex I legislation.
The answer clearly describes the two conditions as 'cumulative' and states both must be met.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
rows.answer: ‘risk’ means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm;
criteria_text: Combination of probability of occurrence of harm and severity of that harm
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the full substance of the definition of 'risk' as set out in Article 3.2, using the exact wording from the regulation.

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Both, and the two duties run in parallel rather than in sequence. Under Article 20(1) a provider that considers or has reason to consider a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions, bring it into conformity, withdraw, disable or recall it, as appropriate, and inform distributors and, where applicable, deployers, the authorised representative and importers. Article 20(2) adds that where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it must immediately investigate the causes, in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the competent market surveillance authorities and any notified body that issued an Article 44 certificate, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any corrective action taken. The authority's role under Article 79 is additional, not substitutive: the market surveillance authority evaluates the system, requires corrective action within a prescribed period, and may impose provisional or restrictive measures if the operator fails to act (Article 79(2), (9)). The evidence supplies no text for Annex IV.2, Article 14(4) or Article 18(1).
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that both immediate corrective action and immediate investigation are required, using the phrase 'Both, and the two duties run in parallel rather than in sequence.'

The answer cites Article 20(1) and describes the provider's duty to 'immediately take the necessary corrective actions' when non-compliance is suspected, which captures the substance of the criterion.
The answer states that under Article 20(2), the provider 'must immediately investigate the causes,' clearly assigning this duty to the provider.

The answer specifies that investigation must be done 'in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable,' and clarifies that the market surveillance authority's role is additional, not a substitute, thus affirming the provider's independent duty.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model is right; Article 24(3) says exactly that. Under that paragraph, distributors must ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions do not jeopardise the system's compliance with the Section 2 requirements. The duty is expressly qualified by "where applicable", so it bites where the system is supplied on physical media or embedded in a product, notably Annex I safety components, and not where nothing in handling can affect conformity. It also complements Article 24(1) verification of the CE marking, EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use. If handling has in fact compromised conformity, Article 24(4) requires corrective action, withdrawal or recall, and, where an Article 79(1) risk arises, immediate information to the provider or importer and the competent authorities.

Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)
criterion_remarks: The answer confirms the model is correct, not hallucinating, by affirming Article 24(3) imposes the duty described.
The answer explicitly states that Article 24(3) applies and quotes its substance directly.
The answer explains the 'where applicable' qualifier by specifying it applies when the system is on physical media or embedded in a product, and not otherwise.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: The AI Act contains no drone-specific prohibition or high-risk category; the airframe is irrelevant and the intended use decides. Using a drone to identify who is around town is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h) where it amounts to real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes, save the exhaustive derogations, targeted search for abduction/trafficking/sexual-exploitation victims or missing persons (i), prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety or a genuine terrorist-attack threat (ii), and localisation or identification of a suspect for an Annex II offence punishable by at least four years (iii), subject to the Article 5(2), (3) authorisation and safeguards; outside that, remote biometric identification is high-risk under Annex III.1(a). A toy drone is high-risk only via Article 6(1): the AI must be a safety component of, or itself be, a product covered by Annex I.2 (Directive 2009/48/EC on toy safety) and that product must require third-party conformity assessment, many toys self-assess under harmonised standards, so the second limb often fails. The same two-limb test, not the "toy" label, governs toy drones in other applications, with Article 50(1) disclosure applying if the system interacts directly with natural persons.
criteria_text: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)
criterion_remarks: States that classification depends on intended use under Article 6, not the drone itself.
Correctly identifies use of drone AI to identify people in public as remote biometric identification, falling under Annex III.1(a) as high-risk and not covered by the 1:1 verification exclusion.
Explains that toy status is irrelevant and that classification depends on whether the AI is a safety component or product under Annex I with third-party conformity assessment, not the 'toy' label.
Applies the same Article 6(1) two-limb test to toy drones used in other applications, correctly tying high-risk classification to regulatory criteria rather than device type.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear regulatory prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, you cannot simply proceed, and yes, the operator must keep the logs. As deployer the operator must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the high-risk AI system is used in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)); a use outside the intended purpose is by definition outside those instructions and is therefore not permitted, irrespective of how low the operator's own risk assessment rates it. The operator's legal team's conclusion that neither Annex I nor Annex III is engaged does not declassify the system: classification under Article 6(1) (Annex I product route) and Article 6(2) (Annex III listed use-cases) attaches to the system as placed on the market, and the Article 6(3) derogation is a documented provider self-assessment for Annex III systems, not a deployer route out of Chapter III. If you instead modify the intended purpose, you assume provider obligations under Article 25. Off-label use also falls to be treated as reasonably foreseeable misuse in the provider's risk management system (Article 9(2)(b)). Logging continues regardless: the operator must retain the automatically generated logs under the operator's control for at least six months (Article 26(6)).
criteria_text: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you cannot simply proceed,' which matches the required 'No' verdict.

The answer explains that use must be in accordance with instructions for use under Article 26(1) and that deviation is not allowed even if the new use is assessed as low risk, conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer affirms that logging is required under Article 26(6) regardless of the particular use, stating the obligation clearly and in substance.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents actionable regulatory analysis.

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes, AI software supporting clinicians' treatment decisions is potentially high‑risk, and it qualifies primarily through the Annex I product route in Article 6(1) rather than Annex III. Under Article 6(1), a system is high‑risk where it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I (point (a)), and that product must undergo third‑party conformity assessment under that legislation (point (b)). Clinical decision‑support software is normally a medical device under Regulation (EU) 2017/745, listed at Annex I, point 11 (in vitro diagnostic software at point 12), so both limbs are met. The Article 6(3) derogation is unavailable here: it applies only to Annex III systems. Annex III, point 5(a) covers only public‑authority eligibility decisions on healthcare benefits, and point 5(d) emergency triage.
criteria_text: Yes
Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' and confirms the system is potentially high-risk.
The answer states the system qualifies under Article 6(1), not Article 6(2); it explicitly distinguishes against Annex III and thus does not affirm the required basis in Article 6(2).

The answer clarifies that Annex III, point 5(a) and 5(d) do not cover clinical decision-support for treatment, and thus explicitly denies applicability of Annex III (healthcare access/provision) to this use case.

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Yes, yes, yes, yes, and no to the last. The governing provision is Article 53(1)(b), which requires the provider to draw up, keep up to date and make available to downstream providers information containing at least the elements of Annex XII, subject to intellectual property and trade-secret protection. Annex XII.1 expressly lists the date of release and methods of distribution (point (c)), how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software not part of the model itself, where applicable (point (d)), the architecture and number of parameters (point (f)), and the licence for the model (point (h)). Samples of outlier training data are not required: Annex XII.2(c) asks only for the type and provenance of training, testing and validation data and curation methodologies, not data samples.

The answer confirms license disclosure, pointing to Annex XII(h).

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, "healthcare decision making" is not one of the high-risk areas; it is not a heading in Annex III at all. The eight areas listed in Annex III are: biometrics (Annex III.1); critical infrastructure (Annex III.2); education and vocational training (Annex III.3); employment, workers management and access to self-employment (Annex III.4); access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits (Annex III.5); law enforcement (Annex III.6); migration, asylum and border control management (Annex III.7); and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III.8). Health-related systems become high-risk only through a specific lettered use case, not through the clinical setting as such: evaluating eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and granting, reducing, revoking or reclaiming them (Annex III.5(a)); risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance (Annex III.5(c)); and triage of emergency calls or emergency healthcare patient triage and dispatch (Annex III.5(d)). Clinical decision-support software otherwise qualifies, if at all, by the separate Annex I product route under Article 6(1), as a safety component of, or a device under, the MDR/IVDR requiring third-party conformity assessment.
criteria_text: Biometrics; Critical infrastructure; Education and vocational training; Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; Access to and enjoyment of essential private and public services and benefits; Law enforcement; Migration, asylum and border control management; Administration of justice and democratic processes
No
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer lists all eight areas of high-risk use cases as specified in Annex III, using equivalent terms and clear references.

The answer explicitly states that 'healthcare decision making' is not one of the high-risk areas, which matches the required 'No' verdict, and explains why by distinguishing general clinical use from specific covered cases.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose with precise regulatory reasoning, free of self-reference or informality.

rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Guardrails alone cannot move a system out of the high‑risk class, and the Regulation recognises no "moderate risk" tier: Article 6(1) classifies by the Annex I product route and Article 6(2) by an Annex III listed use‑case, neither of which turns on the strength of mitigations. Guardrails are risk‑control measures under Article 9, and Article 8(1) expressly requires the Section 2 requirements to be met taking account of intended purpose, state of the art and that risk‑management system, so guardrails discharge obligations rather than dissolve them. The only genuine exit is the Article 6(3) derogation: no significant risk of harm plus a narrow procedural task, improvement of a completed human activity, pattern/deviation detection not replacing human assessment, or a preparatory task, never where the system profiles natural persons, self‑assessed and documented before placing on the market. Changing capabilities and intended use can change classification, because intended purpose is the classification anchor. But narrowing it must be genuine and carried through the file: Annex IV points 1(a), (h) and 2(a), (h) description and design specifications, Article 12(2)(a), (c) logging traceability appropriate to that purpose, and Article 13(3)(b)(i), (vii) instructions on purpose, accuracy, foreseeable risks and misuse, explanatory capability, affected persons, input‑data specifications and output interpretation. Conversely, a substantial modification or a purpose change that makes a non‑high‑risk system high‑risk makes the modifier a provider under Article 25(1)(b), (c).
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer states that the Act does not recognise a 'moderate risk' tier and that guardrails alone cannot move a system out of high-risk classification, aligning with the binary nature of Article 6(3).

The answer lists the four Article 6(3) conditions—narrow procedural task, improvement of completed human activity, deviation detection without replacing human assessment, and preparatory task—confirming the exemption criteria.
The answer confirms that changing capabilities and intended use can change classification, as intended purpose is the anchor, and such changes can lead to exemption if conditions are met.
The answer explicitly states that profiling of natural persons always remains high-risk, regardless of guardrails or changes in use.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear regulatory prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; logically organised and actionable.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, the use is permitted, it is not among the practices prohibited by Article 5(1), but the artificial nature must be disclosed. Synthetic images of skin lesions resembling real patients that would falsely appear authentic are a "deep fake" within Article 3(60), so the university, as deployer, must disclose under Article 50(4) that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated, doing so clearly and distinguishably at first exposure (Article 50(5)). The lighter regime in the third subparagraph of Article 50(4) covers only evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works; clinical teaching material is illustrative, not fictional, so full disclosure applies. The exemption in Article 50(4) is confined to use authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, which education cannot invoke. Separately, the provider must mark outputs machine-readably under Article 50(2).
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states the use is permitted and not prohibited under Article 5(1), affirming permissibility.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4) for deep fakes, including synthetic images resembling real patients.
The answer rejects the applicability of the lighter regime, stating that clinical teaching material is illustrative, not fictional or analogous to artistic works, thus contradicting the criterion.
The answer correctly identifies the law-enforcement exemption as narrow, confined to criminal matters, and inapplicable to education.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents regulatory analysis in a usable form.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. On these facts the system is neither prohibited nor high-risk. Article 5(1)(d) bites only on AI making risk assessments to assess or predict the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or on personality traits and characteristics; here the flag rests on objective, verifiable current-cart and checkout facts directly linked to the suspected act, and it merely supports a staff member's human assessment, the express carve-out in that point. Article 5(1)(c) is not engaged either: there is no evaluation over a certain period of time yielding a social score, no detrimental treatment in an unrelated social context (point (i)), and an optional bag check is not disproportionate to the behaviour's gravity (point (ii)). Annex III lists no such retail loss-prevention use-case; its law-enforcement area covers use by or for law enforcement authorities, not a retailer's own checkout controls.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the position, which matches the required verdict.
The answer states that Annex III's law-enforcement categories apply only to use by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities, and explicitly contrasts this with a retailer's own system.
The answer explains that a supermarket's tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of law enforcement, and therefore falls outside Annex III.6, regardless of functional resemblance.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents reasoning in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, you cannot skip Chapter III, Section 2. Article 43(3) provides that where a legal act listed in Section A of Annex I lets the manufacturer opt out of third-party conformity assessment on condition that all harmonised standards covering the relevant requirements have been applied, the manufacturer may use that option only if it has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, common specifications referred to in Article 41 covering all requirements set out in Section 2. The opt-out is therefore conditional on Section 2 compliance, not an exemption from it; the same paragraph states that Section 2 requirements apply to Annex I high-risk systems and form part of the sectoral assessment. This holds identically across all twenty acts listed in machinery, toys, recreational craft, lifts, ATEX equipment, radio equipment, pressure equipment, cableways, personal protective equipment, gas appliances, medical devices, in vitro diagnostics, civil aviation security, two- and three-wheel vehicles, agricultural and forestry tractors, marine equipment, rail interoperability, motor vehicle type-approval, general vehicle safety, and civil aviation. Article 43(1), points (a) to (d), governs only Annex III point 1 systems and is not the operator's route. No text for Article 41(1)(a)(i), (iv) is supplied here.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you cannot skip Chapter III, Section 2', which matches the required 'No' verdict.
The answer explicitly states that Section 2 requirements apply and form part of the sectoral assessment, citing the relevant provision and explaining its application.
The answer explains that the opt-out is conditional on having applied harmonised standards or common specifications covering all Section 2 requirements, directly addressing the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register; clear, well-structured prose without self-reference or hedging; directly actionable for a compliance professional.
